Kea (Nestor notabilis) hatch from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] for a period of approximately 24.5 days [ab = approximately 24.5 days], an incubation duration that reflects the relatively advanced development of the neonate at hatching. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of 18.7 grams [Wwb = 18.7 grams], a modest initial mass that belies the substantial growth required to reach adult proportions. This altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning for its early development, relying on the rich yolk reserves and subsequent crop milk and food deliveries from both parents.

Development proceeds rapidly under the typical thermal conditions of the nesting cavity, which is maintained near an adult's active metabolic temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Within this thermal regime, a predictable sequence of milestones unfolds: fledging, the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 45 days after hatching [tx = 45 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Shortly after this period, at roughly six and a half weeks of age, the young bird begins to consume solid seeds independently, marking the onset of nutritional independence as parental provisioning wanes. The growing juvenile then enters a prolonged period of somatic maturation before reaching reproductive competence.

Under the same metabolic thermal conditions (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the onset of puberty, defined by gonadal activation and the capacity to breed, is estimated to occur at 135 days after hatching [tp = 135 days after hatching]. This relatively late attainment of sexual maturity for a bird of this size is likely linked to the complex social structure and cognitive demands of the species, as Kea are known for their extended juvenile learning period during which they acquire the manipulative skills necessary to exploit diverse alpine food resources. The pubertal transition coincides with a broadening of the diet and the assumption of adult-like foraging behaviors.

Despite reaching sexual maturity early in their second year, however, first reproduction is typically deferred. The time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which a female lays her first successful clutch, is approximately 3 years [tR = approximately 3 years] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and actual breeding is thought to reflect the challenges of territory establishment, pair-bond formation, and the accumulation of sufficient foraging experience to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and chick rearing. The reproductive rate is consequently low; females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with approximately 4 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 4 clutches each year], limiting the annual reproductive output considerably.

The ultimate wet weight of an adult Kea is approximately 922 grams [Wwi = approximately 922 grams], placing it among the larger members of the parrot family, with field records typically ranging from 800 to 1000 grams. This substantial body mass is supported by a generalist, omnivorous diet. The maximum lifespan in the wild has been documented at 47 years [am = 47 years], an exceptional longevity for a parrot of this size and one that underscores a slow life-history strategy characterized by delayed breeding, low reproductive output, and high adult survival at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. These life-history traits are typical of island-endemic and alpine-adapted psittaciformes, where environmental unpredictability favors extended lifespans and repeated breeding opportunities across many decades.
